difficultyReason: The main conclusion is unmarked and sits at the end of the stimulus, while a subsidiary conclusion in the middle is signaled by 'thus.' Test-takers who latch onto the marked 'thus' clause will pick the trap paraphrase of the intermediate step.
stimulus: Hospital administrators have proposed shortening resident physicians' shifts from 24 hours to 16 hours in order to reduce medical errors. But sleep is not the only determinant of clinical performance; continuity of care is also essential, and shorter shifts mean more handoffs between doctors. Thus, shorter shifts introduce a different kind of error: information lost when one physician transfers a case to another. The administrators' proposal will not achieve what they claim for it.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Shortening resident physicians' shifts will not accomplish the reduction in medical errors that administrators expect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Shorter shifts introduce errors caused by information lost during handoffs between physicians.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sleep deprivation is not the only factor that affects a physician's clinical performance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hospital administrators should abandon any effort to reduce errors made by resident physicians.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Continuity of care is more important to patient outcomes than is the well-rested state of the attending physician.

explanations.correct: The final sentence is the author's main claim; every other sentence — the premise about continuity, and the intermediate conclusion that handoffs cause errors — is offered in support of it.
explanations.B: This is the intermediate conclusion, supported by the continuity-of-care premise and used in turn to support the final sentence. It is the classic subsidiary-conclusion trap.
explanations.C: A premise used to motivate the intermediate conclusion, not the main point.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author attacks this specific proposal, not every error-reduction effort.
explanations.E: Too strong — the author says continuity is also essential, not that it outweighs rest.

difficultyReason: Opens with an opposing view and buries a subsidiary conclusion in the middle of the argument. The author's main conclusion is the last sentence and carries no 'therefore' marker.
stimulus: Some ethicists argue that lying is always wrong because it treats the listener as a mere means to the liar's ends. But consider the physician who withholds a grim prognosis from a patient whose recovery depends on maintaining hope; it follows that some deceptions are performed for the listener's sake rather than the speaker's. The absolutist view mistakes a typical feature of lies for a necessary one.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The claim that lying is always wrong rests on a feature of lies that is common but not essential.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some deceptions are undertaken for the benefit of the person being deceived rather than the benefit of the deceiver.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A physician is justified in withholding a grim prognosis when the patient's recovery depends on hope.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lying is never wrong when it is performed for the listener's sake.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lying treats the listener as a mere means to the liar's ends.

explanations.correct: The last sentence is the author's real claim. The physician example and the intermediate conclusion that some deceptions serve the listener are the support.
explanations.B: This is the intermediate conclusion marked by 'it follows that' — the trap.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author says absolutism is mistaken, not that listener-serving lies are always permissible.
explanations.E: The opposing view the author is rebutting, not the author's own view.

difficultyReason: Conclusion-first structure. The opening sentence is the main claim; a 'thus' clause in the middle marks the subsidiary conclusion and attracts the unwary.
stimulus: Raising the minimum wage in our city will not, on balance, reduce employment among low-wage workers. Studies of recent wage increases in comparable cities show that businesses responded not by firing staff but by modestly raising prices and reducing turnover costs. Thus, the labor savings employers seek come from keeping workers longer, not from employing fewer of them. Any increase in unemployment predicted by simple supply-and-demand models fails to appear when the data are examined.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A higher minimum wage in the city will not, overall, decrease employment of low-wage workers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The labor savings businesses obtain from higher wages come from reduced turnover, not a smaller workforce.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Simple supply-and-demand models do not accurately predict the effects of minimum-wage increases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raising the minimum wage benefits low-wage workers without imposing any cost on employers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Businesses in comparable cities raised prices modestly after recent minimum-wage increases.

explanations.correct: The first sentence states the author's main claim, and everything after it — the study findings, the 'thus' clause about turnover, and the rebuttal of simple models — is offered as support.
explanations.B: The subsidiary conclusion marked by 'thus.' It supports the main claim but is not the main claim.
explanations.C: A supporting point, not the main claim.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author concedes prices and turnover costs shift.
explanations.E: A premise cited from the studies.

difficultyReason: The stimulus presents a legal argument with an intermediate conclusion flagged by 'so.' The main conclusion, at the end, uses a normative verb ('should') without any conclusion marker.
stimulus: Under current law, search warrants must describe with particularity the items officers intend to seize. A warrant that authorizes seizure of 'all documents relating to the defendant's business' fails this requirement, since virtually any paper in the defendant's office could be said to relate to the business. So such a warrant confers on officers the very discretion the particularity rule was meant to restrain. Warrants phrased in this sweeping way should be struck down.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Warrants that authorize seizure of all documents relating to the defendant's business ought to be invalidated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A warrant for 'all documents relating to the defendant's business' gives officers the discretion the particularity rule was designed to prevent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The particularity requirement is intended to restrain officer discretion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No search warrant that fails the particularity requirement can ever be enforced by a court.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Virtually any paper in a defendant's office could be described as relating to the business.

explanations.correct: The final sentence is the author's prescriptive claim; everything before it — the statement of the rule, the example, and the 'so' clause — supports that prescription.
explanations.B: The subsidiary conclusion introduced by 'so.' A trap for readers who stop at the conclusion marker.
explanations.C: A premise explaining the purpose of the rule.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author addresses sweeping business-document warrants, not every warrant that could fail particularity.
explanations.E: A supporting observation, not the main claim.

difficultyReason: The author's main conclusion sits at the end with no marker, while the sentence preceding it carries the 'hence' signpost and is the subsidiary conclusion most students mistake for the main one.
stimulus: Conservationists have urged governments to create more protected reserves to halt species loss. But most species extinctions in recent decades have occurred not inside reserves but along the unprotected edges where reserves meet farmland and roads. Hence the greatest threat to biodiversity is not the absence of reserves but the character of the landscape surrounding them. Expanding reserves without changing what lies outside their borders will do little to stem the decline.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creating additional reserves, without altering conditions in the adjacent landscape, will do little to prevent continued species loss.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The principal danger to biodiversity is the nature of the land surrounding reserves rather than any shortage of reserves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most recent species extinctions have taken place along the unprotected edges of reserves.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Conservationists are wrong to concern themselves with protected reserves at all.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Governments should devote their conservation funding primarily to the management of farmland and roads.

explanations.correct: The last sentence is the author's main claim. The edge-extinction premise and the 'hence' intermediate conclusion together support it.
explanations.B: The subsidiary conclusion marked by 'hence.' The most common trap.
explanations.C: A premise the 'hence' clause is drawn from.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author says more reserves alone won't help, not that reserves are worthless.
explanations.E: Too strong and too specific — the author doesn't recommend a particular funding allocation.

difficultyReason: A technology stimulus in which the subsidiary conclusion is introduced by 'thus' in the middle of the argument and the main conclusion, stated at the end, challenges a popular claim without a conclusion marker.
stimulus: Advocates of facial-recognition systems insist that the technology will make public spaces safer. In controlled laboratory settings, the software misidentifies suspects less than one percent of the time. But in deployed conditions — variable lighting, crowds, movement — independent audits find error rates above ten percent. Thus the accuracy figures quoted by advocates describe performance the technology does not actually deliver in the field. The case for widespread adoption rests on numbers that do not reflect how these systems will be used.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arguments for adopting facial-recognition systems rely on accuracy figures that do not correspond to actual field conditions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The accuracy numbers advocates cite describe performance the technology does not achieve in deployment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Facial-recognition software has error rates above ten percent when used in real-world conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Facial-recognition technology cannot make public spaces safer under any conditions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Laboratory testing of facial-recognition software should be replaced entirely by field testing.

explanations.correct: The last sentence is the author's main charge against the case for adoption; the lab/field contrast and the 'thus' clause both support it.
explanations.B: The intermediate conclusion flagged by 'thus.' It supports the main claim but is not it.
explanations.C: A premise from the audit evidence.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author attacks the case for adoption, not the possibility of benefit.
explanations.E: Beyond the scope — the author doesn't prescribe a testing regime.

difficultyReason: The stimulus opens with the main conclusion; a subsidiary conclusion marked 'it follows that' sits in the middle. Test-takers drawn to the marker will select the intermediate paraphrase.
stimulus: The recent decline of regional dialects in our country cannot be blamed, as some linguists have claimed, on broadcast media. Surveys show that the features of regional speech began to fade earliest in communities where residents routinely traveled to distant cities for work — long before television reached those areas. It follows that sustained face-to-face contact with speakers of other dialects, not exposure to a standardized broadcast voice, is what erodes regional speech. Whatever role television has played, it has been at most an accelerant of a process already underway.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Broadcast media cannot be held responsible for the recent decline of regional dialects in the country.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Face-to-face contact with speakers of other dialects, rather than exposure to broadcast speech, is what wears away regional speech.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Regional speech features began to fade earliest in communities whose residents traveled to distant cities for work.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Television has had no effect whatsoever on the decline of regional dialects.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Broadcast media have slightly accelerated a process of dialect decline that was already underway.

explanations.correct: The first sentence is the author's main claim, rebutting the linguists. Everything that follows — the survey evidence, the 'it follows that' clause, and the concession about television — supports that rebuttal.
explanations.B: The subsidiary conclusion introduced by 'it follows that.' The prime trap.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author concedes television may have been an accelerant.
explanations.E: A concession the author makes in support of the main claim, not the main claim itself.

difficultyReason: A historical stimulus where the final sentence is the main conclusion and an intermediate 'so' clause in the middle offers a competing paraphrase target.
stimulus: It is often said that the invention of the printing press caused the Protestant Reformation. Yet the doctrinal disputes that drove the Reformation had circulated in manuscript form for nearly a century before Luther, and several earlier movements attracted mass followings without the aid of print. So print alone cannot explain why one set of reformist ideas succeeded where earlier ones failed. Historians who treat the press as the decisive cause are mistaking the medium for the message.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Historians err when they treat the printing press as the decisive cause of the Protestant Reformation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The printing press by itself cannot account for the success of Reformation ideas over earlier reformist movements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Doctrinal disputes driving the Reformation had circulated in manuscript form for nearly a century before Luther.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The printing press played no role at all in the spread of Protestant ideas during the Reformation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The true cause of the Reformation's success was the content of its doctrines rather than the channels through which they spread.

explanations.correct: The last sentence is the author's target claim about historians; the manuscript premise and the 'so' intermediate both support it.
explanations.B: The intermediate conclusion marked by 'so' — the subsidiary-conclusion trap.
explanations.C: A historical premise used in support.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author denies the press was decisive, not that it mattered at all.
explanations.E: A different claim the author does not actually make; goes beyond the critique of historians.

difficultyReason: Policy argument in which the main conclusion is the final sentence, left unmarked, and a 'thus' clause midway through yields an attractive subsidiary paraphrase.
stimulus: City officials have defended their congestion-pricing plan on the grounds that it will reduce traffic. But when similar plans were introduced in other cities, downtown traffic did fall while overall regional traffic simply shifted to unpriced corridors nearby. Thus congestion pricing tends to relocate traffic rather than eliminate it. The plan, sold to residents as a remedy for the region's congestion problem, will not actually solve it.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The congestion-pricing plan will not, in fact, solve the region's congestion problem as its proponents claim.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Congestion pricing typically redistributes traffic to nearby unpriced corridors rather than eliminating it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In other cities that adopted similar plans, downtown traffic fell even as overall regional traffic did not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The congestion-pricing plan will have no effect whatsoever on traffic patterns in the region.

choices.label: E
choices.text: City officials should never have proposed the congestion-pricing plan in the first place.

explanations.correct: The final sentence states the author's main claim about the plan; the experience from other cities and the 'thus' generalization both support it.
explanations.B: The intermediate conclusion marked by 'thus' — the subsidiary-conclusion trap.
explanations.C: A premise drawn from experience elsewhere.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author says the plan will shift traffic, not that it has no effect.
explanations.E: A prescriptive claim the author does not actually make.

difficultyReason: An arts stimulus with an opposing view at the start and a 'thus' subsidiary conclusion in the middle. The author's main conclusion is the last sentence and carries no explicit marker.
stimulus: Some critics claim that the value of a novel lies in the moral lessons it imparts to its readers. But great novels often portray morally repugnant characters without condemning them, and readers of such novels emerge not with neat lessons but with a richer sense of human complexity. Thus what readers take from the best fiction is something other than moral instruction. Judging novels by the lessons they teach is to measure them against a standard their authors never set out to meet.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Evaluating novels by the moral lessons they offer holds them to a standard their authors did not set for themselves.

choices.label: B
choices.text: What readers gain from the best fiction is something other than moral instruction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many great novels depict morally repugnant characters without passing judgment on them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The value of a novel consists in the moral lessons it imparts to its readers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Novels that attempt to offer moral lessons cannot be considered great works of fiction.

explanations.correct: The last sentence is the author's main claim about how novels should be judged. The premise about repugnant characters and the 'thus' intermediate both support it.
explanations.B: The subsidiary conclusion marked by 'thus' — the primary trap.
explanations.D: The opposing view the author is rebutting, not the author's own view.
explanations.E: Too strong — the author rejects moral instruction as the measure of a novel, not as compatible with greatness.
